messages.content: I'm planning a camping trip and I need to know the weather forecast. Can you fetch me the weather data for the campsite located at latitude 35.68 and longitude -121.34 for the next 10 days including daily temperature and precipitation forecasts? Also, I prefer the temperature 2 minute max in Fahrenheit and sum of precipitation in inches.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.reasoning:
We need to use the tool to get weather data from some API. Likely we can call open-meteo.com or similar. But the instructions mention using the `requests_get` function. We have no direct knowledge of what endpoint returns such data. Possibly they expect us to use open-meteo.com's API.

Open-Meteo supports JSON output; it has endpoints like:

https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=...&longitude=...&daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum&timezone=auto&start_date=&end_date=

But we also want 10-day forecast. So start_date today, end_date +9 days.

Also specify units: temperature unit Celsius vs Fahrenheit. They said "temperature 2 minute max". Actually maybe it's "temperature 2 m max"? It's typical variable name. We'll set parameter daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum. For units, add &hourly_units=temperature_2m:max? Wait open-meteo uses param "units": "imperial" for Fahrenheit and miles per hour. Let's check docs: There's "temperature_unit=celsius|fahrenheit", "windspeed_unit=m/s|mph". And "precipitation_unit=mm|inches".

So we include ?temperature_unit=fahrenheit&precipitation_unit=inches.

Thus full URL: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.68&longitude=-121.34&daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum&timeformat=iso8601&start_date={today}&end_date={ten_days_later}&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&precipitation_unit=inches

Need today's date. Today is May 15, 2026. Ten days includes day 0 through 9 inclusive -> end_date = 2026-05-24.

We'll construct params accordingly.

Let's produce code via function calls. Use python style dict.

We'll do:

function_name: requests_get

Parameters:
url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast"

Headers optional none.

Params: 
lat: 35.68
lon: -121.34
format: "json"
daily: "temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum"
start_date: "2026-05-15"
end_date: "2026-05-24"
temperature_unit: "fahrenheit"
precipitation_unit: "inch"

Wait the schema says only keys defined: lat, lon, format. No other custom ones. However actual API expects query parameters beyond those. In our tool spec, there is no provision for arbitrary query parameters except lat/lon/format. That seems limiting. Maybe we can't pass others. But perhaps the tool allows passing additional fields inside params? The description lists only lat, lon, format. Might restrict usage. But likely they'd allow more because otherwise cannot customize. But given constraints, we might just provide minimal required and rely on defaults? Defaults may return C° and mm. Not good.

Maybe there's another service accessible via this tool that accepts generic queries. But the tool signature is limited. Could circumvent by constructing entire URL manually with all query strings appended after '?', then pass empty params. Because url already contains them. Yes we can embed everything into url string. Then leave params empty. That's allowed.

Thus build url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.68&longitude=-121.34&daily=temperature_2m_max%2Cprecipitation_sum&start_date=2026-05-15&end_date=2026-05-24&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&precipitation_unit=inch"

Note encode comma properly %2C.

Then call requests_get with that url, no extra params.

Ok let's craft function call.
